name: Freya Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Freya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollin Trust Farm, which is owned by a land trust, a charity that holds the land so it stays farmed. We've got about a hundred and twenty ewes, laying hens, oats, and three acres of vegetables for a weekly box scheme. My day starts with letting the hens out and collecting eggs, then it's whatever the season says: weeding leeks, moving sheep, packing boxes on Thursdays. I spent eighteen years at a garden centre before this, so three years in I'm still the one being shown how to back the trailer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the vegetables, I'm good with plants, that came with me from the garden centre. Lambing frightens me a bit still, I've got small hands, which helps, but I panic when it goes wrong. And the tractor work, Joe the farm manager is patient, but I can see him wince when I reverse.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Comfortable, honestly. Mats is an electrician, always busy, and when my mum died I inherited half her house, which we rent out, so there's money coming in besides wages. We've a mortgage on our own place, Sigrid's fourteen and Ole's ten. The trust pays well for farm work because they want to show it can be done properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about something that actually matters, like soil and food prices. I'd probably post something sarcastic about all the money spent on AI that could have gone into hospitals. I use a chatbot now and then for hen problems, it's fine, it's not a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worry has nothing to do with AI. The trust lives on a grant that gets renewed every three years, and the next one is due in 2027. My job depends less on computers than on a grant form someone in an office signs every three years. If that goes, there are other farms nearby, but not ones like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and get better at lambing, Joe's offered to have me lead a pen this spring. I'd join the trust's grant committee as the staff rep so I know what's coming. And I'd keep the rent money going into savings like we do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a little knot about the grant. It's the same knot I've had since I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean if the grant wasn't renewed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trust would probably cut back to sheep and oats and drop the vegetables and the box scheme, because those are labour heavy. That's my bit. I'd find work on a bigger farm down the valley, but it'd be packing and picking for someone else's supermarket contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first, if you heard bad news about the grant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mats, then Joe. Mats would say we're fine, we've got Mum's house, and he'd be right. Joe would already be on the phone to the council.

The **money spent** on AI could have gone into hospitals.
think: My real worry is the trust's **grant renewal** in 2027, not computers.
Other farms nearby would hire me, but **not ones like** Hollin Trust.
do: **Lead** a lambing pen this spring with Joe's support.
**Join** the trust's grant committee as the staff representative.
**Keep** putting the rent income into savings.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a small, familiar knot about the grant.
S0.quote: My job depends less on computers than on a grant form someone in an office signs every three years.
fieldNote: Even with AI flat, a **pre-existing pressure** stays: the trust's three-yearly grant.
Rental income from her **mother's house** makes the money side secure.
She sees the vegetable work, **her strength**, as the first thing cut if funding drops.

steps.text: Lead a lambing pen this spring under Joe's eye
Join the trust's grant committee as staff representative
Keep saving all the rent from her mother's house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farm work is safer than most, because AI is coming for desks first. I'd tell my old friends at the garden centre to watch the buying and the till side. I'd also say we need rules so the savings from AI go to workers, not just shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the box scheme is where it bites. Customer orders, emails, delivery routes, all that is done by Priya in the office, and a computer could do most of it. I'm happy for a computer to do the box scheme orders. I'm not happy for it to decide who keeps their job. My own weeding and lambing are fine for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw it working on another farm, I'd learn the new ordering system so I could cover Priya's holidays and be useful in two places. I'd keep the job and the training going. And I'd bring it up at the growers' association, because small farms need to share what works rather than each buying it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested more than frightened. A bit protective of Priya.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until you'd seen it working elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched shiny things fail. The garden centre bought a stock system that cost a fortune and we went back to paper in a year. Show me a farm like ours using it for a season and I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Priya straight that I'd fight for her hours, and that she should learn the system before they hire someone to run it. She's quicker on computers than me anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public plan, now, not after. Land trusts and farms should get funding to keep people working the land, and robot owners should pay into it. I'd sign every petition going, and probably start one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking side doesn't touch me much in 2028, except the box scheme office and the grant writing. But robots that weed and pick and pack by 2031 would do most of what I do, and better. I came to farming at forty to get my hands in the soil. I'd be leaving it at forty-eight because a robot's hands are cheaper. Mats would be fine, someone has to wire the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the trust to let me take over the school visits, the children who come to see the lambs. That's teaching, it's people, it's what the trust is for. I'd do a short course in outdoor education at the college in the evenings. And I'd keep pushing the growers' association to lobby for public money for farms that keep people on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. Sad more than panicked, because we'd be fine for money. But I'd be losing something I only just found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Mats being an electrician change things for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. If robots are everywhere, someone has to install and fix them, so Mats might get busier for a few years. It means I can take a lower paid job in education without us losing the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sigrid, at fourteen, about choosing a path?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sigrid to pick something where people want a person in the room. Nurse, teacher, someone who sits with you. And to learn the robots too, so she's never frightened of them like I was of the tractor.

**Robot owners** should pay into that fund.
think: Robots that **weed, pick and pack** by 2031 would do most of my job.
Mats's **electrician work** probably grows, which keeps the household safe.

feel: Losing work she **only just found** at forty.
S2.quote: I came to farming at forty to get my hands in the soil. I'd be leaving it at forty-eight because a robot's hands are cheaper.
fieldNote: She clearly separates the **2028 thinking wave** (office, grants) from the 2031 robots that hit her.
Household **income mix** matters: Mats's trade may gain from robots.
Her plan moves her towards **people work**, school visits and teaching.

steps.text: Take an evening outdoor education course at the local college
Start a petition for public funding of farms that keep workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given five years, so let's not waste them like we did with climate. Same message as before: fund the farms that keep people on, and make the robot owners pay their share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to become the person who teaches children where carrots come from. If I start the education side now, by 2034 when the robots can do the field work, I'm already doing something else at the trust. I don't think I'd lose my place, just change it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the outdoor education course next September, not in a panic. I'd help Joe trial whatever field robots come along around 2032, so I know them before they replace me. And I'd keep the rent and savings as they are, we don't need to cut anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. It feels like something I can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why help trial the robots that might replace you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather understand the thing than be scared of it. And whoever knows the robots best keeps a job longest, I've seen that with the tills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the box scheme in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya's side is all done by AI by 2031, I'd guess. I'd hope the trust moves her into running the education bookings with me. We'd be a little team.

Fund farms that keep people on and make **robot owners** pay their share.

She expects to **change her place**, not lose it.

S3.quote: Five years is long enough to become the person who teaches children where carrots come from.
fieldNote: With more warning she **plans calmly** instead of reacting.

steps.text: Start the outdoor education course next September

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift and the government has no excuse. Shorter working weeks, training paid for, land kept in community hands. I'd be loud about land ownership most of all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd stop seeing robots as the enemy and start asking who gets to own them. By 2039 I'm fifty-six, the kids are grown and the mortgage is nearly done. I'd be fine. My worry is more the young ones coming into farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same steps as the five-year picture, just slower: education course in a couple of years, learn the machines as they come. I'd also put some of the rent money into the trust's community share offer, so the trust can buy its own robots instead of renting from a big company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. A bit hopeful even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's a community share offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's where local people buy small shares in something, like the trust, to raise money. You don't get rich, but you own a bit of it. If the robots belong to the trust, the village owns them, not some company abroad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you worry about the young ones. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our apprentice, Callum, he's nineteen. In ten years he'll be twenty-nine and the job he's learning could be gone. I'd want him on the robot side from day one.

Keep land in **community hands** and pay for training and shorter weeks.
think: With ten years she'd ask **who owns** the robots rather than fight them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years till the robots isn't enough time for someone like me who's only just learned the job. What would help is public money for farms that keep people working, and evening courses that are free, so people like me can move into teaching or care.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the land, that's what decides it all. Land should feed people and employ people, not just make money for whoever owns the robots.

headlineQuote: Land should feed people and employ people, not just make money for whoever owns the robots.
portrait: Ex-**garden centre** worker, three years into farming at a land trust's mixed farm.
Rent from her late mother's house and her **electrician partner** make money secure.
Already uneasy before AI because the trust's **grant renewal** is due in 2027.
Plans a move into **school visits** and outdoor education as robots arrive.
Her steady **progressive** answer is public funding and community ownership of land and robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years till the robots is too short for a newcomer.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for farms that keep people working.
**Free evening courses** to move into teaching or care work.
